newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech opposition boss rejects closet communist tag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech opposition boss rejects closet communist tag.

text.p: Czech Social Democrat chairman Milos Zeman compares himself with British Labour leader Tony Blair and his party with any Western centre-left group you care to name. Reform communism has no place in his vocabulary.
But with the Social Democrats tantalisingly close to their first election victory since the fall of communism, Zeman's enemies accuse him of trying to turn back the clock on reform.

Doubts are also growing over Zeman's ability to hold his party together after a parliamentary rebellion by four Social Democrat deputies last month followed by a slanging match between centrist and ex-communist members.

The Social Democrats, who have been running neck and neck with the ruling Civic Democratic Party (ODS) for Senate elections starting this weekend, are still fighting accusations that they are fundamentally opposed to the free market.

Zeman, a 52-year-old economist, therefore likens himself to Blair, who dragged his party into the political centre and stands a strong chance next year of becoming Britain's first Labour prime minister for almost two decades.
Unlike their reformed communist counterparts in Poland, Hungary and Slovakia, the Czech Social Democrats were reborn after 1989 as a Western-style centre-left party, he says.
Zeman rejects any suggestion that he is a bogeyman who will frighten off the foreign investment still needed to rebuild the Czech economy after 40 years of communism.

"Foreign business doesn't hold any fear in the case of Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and other Social Democratic countries," he said before lower house elections earlier this year. "Why be afraid afraid in the case of a Social Democratic party in the government of the Czech Republic?"

Zeman was once a communist, but as a student during the "Prague Spring" democratic reforms of 1968. He was expelled from the party in the purges which followed the Soviet-led invasion of the country the same year.
This June's elections were an outstanding success for Zeman, a bushy-haired heavy smoker.
After a strong campaign touring the country by bus, the Social Democrats stunned the nation by stripping the centre- right coalition of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus of its majority.
Klaus remained in power because Zeman could not form a coalition with the two other opposition parties, the little reformed Communist and the far-right Republicans.
But Zeman has used his position as lower house speaker to harass Klaus, a long-standing personal enemy.

So far his record has been impressive. He has transformed the Social Democrats from also-rans who won just 6.5 percent of the vote in 1992 elections to a force which took 26 percent in June, only three percentage points behind Klaus's ODS.
Since then, most opinion polls have put the Social Democrats virtually level on about 26 percent each.

Klaus, no doubt alarmed by the Social Democrats' progress, has accused Zeman of jeopardising everything that has been achieved since the "Velvet Revolution" which began in November 1989 and toppled communism in weeks.

"Social Democracy presents a fundamental questioning of the entire post-November development," he said. "(The Social Democrats) are casting doubt on the fundamental view of the economy, privatisation, social policy and seeks again the paternalistic system of the past where the state is above all."
The Social Democrats have no policy to reverse privatisation, although they want to halt the sale of state hospitals.

They even accept Klaus's concept of a balanced budget for the time being, although they believe that a modest deficit within limits laid down by the European Union's Maastricht Treaty is acceptable for modernising the country.
Zeman also favours EU membership and joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), although he says there should be a referendum on that issue.
But sometimes his comments seem rambling and contradictory and his leadership may be his weakness.
Last month divisions among Social Democrats burst into the open when four deputies joined the Klaus government in parliament to vote for the first reading of the 1997 budget.
One prominent Social Democrat, Michal Kraus, accused the four, who included party vice-chairman Karel Machovec, of being "corrupted politically" by the ODS.
The rebels responded by threatening legal action and questioned the past of Kraus, who was a hard-line Communist Party parliamentarian before 1989.

Instead of stifling the infighting, Zeman joined in. At a news conference he flatly denied there was any split in the ranks and then threatened to resign unless the party dimissed Machovec as vice-chairman at a congress next year.
The squabbling may have taken its toll and a recent opinion poll showed ODS had pulled ahead again before the Senate elections with 25.4 percent to the Social Democrats' 20.2.

But Zeman sharply rejects Klaus's accusation that he is turning back the clock on reform. "The prime minister is not telling the truth, which I can prove," he said. "This is a serious thing in any democratic country."
